validated.name: Insecure Direct Object Reference (BOLA)
validated.description: Object referenced by 'id=1' is returned to identity 'bob' even though it belongs to 'alice'. The endpoint enforces no object-level authorization, so any authenticated user can read other users' records by changing the identifier (IDOR/BOLA).
validated.evidence: 'alice' and 'bob' received byte-equivalent object-specific responses for id=1 (similarity 1.00), while a bogus id (7000004) returned HTTP 404 / distinct content — proving the response is object-specific, not a generic page.
validated.poc:
As user 'bob' (not the owner), request:
  GET http://127.0.0.1:8000/profile?id=1
  -> HTTP 200 containing 'alice'-owned data.

curl -sS -i -H 'Cookie: session=bob' 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/profile?id=1'
validated.remediation: Enforce an authorization check on every object access: verify the authenticated principal owns or may access the requested object before returning it. Do not rely on the identifier being unguessable.

validated.name: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting
validated.description: The 'q' parameter is reflected into the HTML response without output encoding, allowing arbitrary HTML/JavaScript injection that executes in the victim's browser (reflected XSS).
validated.evidence:
Parameter 'q' reflected the injected markup 't5d02232f"'>' into the HTML response body without entity-encoding (the characters < > " ' survived intact). Reflection context excerpt: ...ults for: t5d02232f"'>

No results.

...
validated.poc:
GET http://127.0.0.1:8000/search?q=%22%3E%3Csvg+onload%3Dalert%28document.domain%29%3E

Open the URL above in a browser; the injected <svg onload> fires in the page's origin. Reproduce with:
curl -sS -i 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/search?q=%22%3E%3Csvg+onload%3Dalert%28document.domain%29%3E'
validated.remediation: Contextually output-encode the parameter when writing it into HTML (HTML-entity encode <, >, ", ', &). Prefer the framework's auto-escaping templating. Add a restrictive Content-Security-Policy as defence in depth.

validated.name: Open Redirect
validated.description: The 'url' parameter controls the redirect destination without validating it against an allow-list. An attacker can send victims a trusted-looking link that silently forwards them to an arbitrary external site (phishing, OAuth token theft).
validated.evidence: Request to http://127.0.0.1:8000/go?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftalon-oredir.example.com%2Fpoc returned HTTP 302 with Location: https://talon-oredir.example.com/poc — the server redirected to the attacker-controlled host 'talon-oredir.example.com'.
validated.poc:
GET http://127.0.0.1:8000/go?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftalon-oredir.example.com%2Fpoc
-> HTTP 302, Location: https://talon-oredir.example.com/poc

curl -sS -i 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/go?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftalon-oredir.example.com%2Fpoc'   # note: no -L, so the 3xx Location is visible
validated.remediation: Do not place user input directly in the redirect target. Validate against a server-side allow-list of permitted paths/hosts, or map an opaque key to the destination. If external redirects are required, show an interstitial.
